title: Doing something for each item
objectives: Loop over a range and over a list with `for`.
Collect a running total or a count with an accumulator.

screens.title: One item at a time
screens.prose:
Square brackets hold several values in order: a **list**. Here are four trades' P&Ls in pounds. The `for` line hands the values to the name `p`, one per pass.

```python
pnls = [12.50, -4.00, 7.25, 3.00]
for p in pnls:
    print(p)
```
screens.question: Tap the value `p` holds on the second pass.

hints.text: On the first pass `p` is 12.50, the first value. Where does the arrow go next?
The passes take the values in order, left to right.
The second pass takes the second value, −4.00.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The passes walk the list left to right, one value each.

byKey.c0: That is the first pass. Each pass moves `p` one value to the right.
byKey.c2: You skipped a value. The second pass takes the second value, −4.00.
byKey.c3: That is the last pass. The second pass takes the second value.

explain.text: Pass 1 gives `p` 12.5, pass 2 gives −4.0, then 7.25 and 3.0. When the list runs out, the loop ends: there is no counter or test to write. This is a **`for` loop**.

screens.title: Counting with range
screens.prose:
`range` makes a run of whole numbers for a `for` loop to walk through.

```python
for i in range(4):
    print(i)
```
screens.question: What does it print?

options.why: You started at 1. `range(4)` starts at 0 and gives four numbers.
You included 4. `range(4)` stops before 4, so it gives four numbers, not five.
You printed the 4 itself. The loop runs once per number in the range, printing each.

hints.text: How many numbers does `range(4)` hold? The diagram shows its cells.
`range` starts at 0 unless told otherwise.
Four numbers starting from 0: 0, 1, 2 and 3. Each pass prints one.

feedback.correct: Four numbers, from 0 up to but not including 4.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. `range(4)` has four numbers, and the first is 0.

explain.text: `range(4)` hands the loop 0, 1, 2 and 3: four numbers, starting at 0 and stopping before 4. `range(a, b)` starts at `a` instead and still stops before `b`.

screens.title: A running total
screens.prose:
One variable can collect a result as the loop walks the list. Step through and watch `total`.

```python
pnls = [12.50, -4.00, 7.25, 3.00]
total = 0
for p in pnls:
    total = total + p
print(total)
```

steps.caption: Pass 4: `p` is 3.00, so `total` becomes 15.75 + 3.00 = 18.75. The list is used up, so `print(total)` shows 18.75.

screens.title: Adding up a range
screens.prose:
The same running total, now over `range(1, 6)`.

```python
total = 0
for k in range(1, 6):
    total = total + k
print(total)
```
screens.question: What does it print?

hints.text: Which numbers does `range(1, 6)` hand out?
It starts at 1 and stops before 6.
The numbers are 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5. Add them.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. List the numbers in `range(1, 6)`, then add them.

byKey.with-six: You included 6. `range(1, 6)` stops before 6, so the last number is 5.
byKey.last: You gave the last value of `k`. `total` collects every value, so print shows the sum.
byKey.from-zero: You used 0 to 4, which is `range(5)`. `range(1, 6)` starts at 1.

explain.text: `range(1, 6)` gives 1 to 5, and `total` collects each one. This running-total variable is an **accumulator**: it starts before the loop, and every pass adds to it.

screens.title: Counting up days
screens.prose:
Six daily returns, in %. The `if` inside the loop decides which days count.

```python
returns = [0.8, -1.2, 0.0, 2.1, -0.4, 0.3]
ups = 0
for r in returns:
    if r > 0:
        ups = ups + 1
print(ups)
```
screens.question: Tap every day that adds 1 to `ups`.

hints.text: On each pass, ask the `if` question: is this return above 0?
Look closely at the 0.0 day.
0.8, 2.1 and 0.3 are above 0. 0.0 is not above 0, and the negative days are not either.

feedback.correct: Three up days, so `ups` ends at 3.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Tap a day only when `r > 0` is True for it.

byKey.flat: You counted the 0.0 day. `0.0 > 0` is `False`: a flat day is not an up day.
byKey.c2: You counted the 0.0 day. `0.0 > 0` is `False`: a flat day is not an up day.
byKey.c1: −1.2 is below 0, so `r > 0` is `False` on that pass.
byKey.c4: −0.4 is below 0, so `r > 0` is `False` on that pass.

explain.text: The `if` runs on every pass, but `ups` only grows when its test is `True`: for 0.8, 2.1 and 0.3. The flat day, 0.0, fails `r > 0`. So the program prints 3.

screens.title: The total that forgets
screens.prose:
A colleague moved one line of the running total.

```python
pnls = [12.50, -4.00, 7.25, 3.00]
for p in pnls:
    total = 0
    total = total + p
print(total)
```
screens.question: What does it print?

options.why: You expected the total of all four. `total = 0` is inside the loop now, so it wipes the total at the start of every pass.
The reset comes before the addition on each pass, so the last pass leaves 0 + 3.00, not 0.

options.text: An error: `total` is used before it exists
options.why: `total = 0` runs on every pass before `total + p`, so `total` always exists when it is used.

hints.text: Which lines run on every pass?
`total = 0` is indented, so it runs on every one of these passes.
Each pass sets `total` to 0, then adds that pass's `p`. After the last pass, `total` is 0 + 3.00.

feedback.correct: Each pass starts from 0, so only the last P&L survives.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Run the block for the last pass and see what `total` holds.

byKey.sum: You expected the sum. The reset is inside the loop, so every pass throws the running total away.

explain.text:
`total = 0` sits inside the block, so each pass starts again from 0 and only the last P&L, 3.00, survives. Lines before the `for` run once; lines inside run every pass.

```python
total = 0          # moved up: runs once
for p in pnls:
    total = total + p
```

screens.title: Add the first n numbers
screens.prose: Write a loop that adds the whole numbers from 1 up to and including `n`. So `sum_to(5)` is 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 = 15.
screens.question: Complete `sum_to` with a `for` loop over a `range`.

widget.starter:
def sum_to(n):
    total = 0
    # add 1, 2, ..., n to total with a for loop
    
    return total
widget.how: Check runs 5 hidden tests. `sum_to(0)` must return 0.

hints.text: Which `range` hands out 1, 2, ..., `n`?
`range(1, n)` stops before `n`. You need one more.
Write `for k in range(1, n + 1):` and, indented under it, `total = total + k`.

feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Check `sum_to(5)`: if you get 10, your range stops at 4.

byKey.test-1: `sum_to(5)` should be 15. If you got 10, the range stops before 5: use `range(1, n + 1)`.

explain.text:
`range(1, n + 1)` starts at 1 and stops before `n + 1`, so its last number is `n`. For `n` = 0 it is empty, the loop never runs, and `total` stays 0.

```python
def sum_to(n):
    total = 0
    for k in range(1, n + 1):
        total = total + k
    return total
```

screens.title: The accumulator pattern
screens.prose:
Every total you built had the same shape. Start once, before the loop; add once per item, inside it. For a list $p_1, p_2, \ldots, p_n$ it computes $p_1 + p_2 + \cdots + p_n$.

```python
total = 0              # once, before the loop
for p in pnls:
    total = total + p  # once per item
```

`range(n)` gives 0 to n − 1; `range(a, b)` gives a to b − 1.
screens.question: Which `range` gives the months 1 to 12?

options.why: That gives 0 to 11: twelve numbers, but starting at 0.
That stops before 12, so it gives 1 to 11.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The second number in `range` is the first one left out.

explain.text: `range(1, 13)` starts at 1 and stops before 13, so its last number is 12. The count is `b − a` whenever `b` is at least `a`: here 13 − 1 = 12 months.

screens.title: A day's P&L
screens.prose: At the close, a desk adds up every trade's P&L to get the day's result. Some days there are no trades, and the list is empty.
screens.question: Complete `total_pnl` so it returns the sum of the list.

widget.starter:
def total_pnl(pnls):
    total = 0
    # add each trade's P&L to total
    
    return total
widget.how: Check runs 5 hidden tests on lists of P&Ls in pounds. Answers are compared with `math.isclose`, so tiny float rounding is fine. An empty list must give 0.

hints.text: Which pattern collects a total over a list?
`total` already starts at 0, before the loop. Add one line per trade inside a `for` loop.
Write `for p in pnls:` and, indented under it, `total = total + p`.

feedback.correct: All five tests passed, including the day with no trades.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Check that `total = 0` is still above the loop, not inside it.

explain.text:
The accumulator starts at 0 and each trade adds to it. An empty list means the loop never runs, so the day's P&L is £0.00, which is the right answer for a day with no trades.

```python
def total_pnl(pnls):
    total = 0
    for p in pnls:
        total = total + p
    return total
```

screens.title: Hit rate of a signal
screens.prose: A quick check on a strategy is how many days it made money. Count the up days in a list of daily returns: days strictly above 0.
screens.question: Complete `up_days`.

widget.starter:
def up_days(returns):
    count = 0
    # add 1 to count for each return above 0
    
    return count
widget.how: Check runs 6 hidden tests on lists of daily returns in %. A return of exactly 0 is not an up day, and an empty list has 0 up days.

hints.text: You need a loop over the list with an `if` inside it.
The `if` line goes inside the `for` block, and the counting line inside the `if` block: two indents.
Write `for r in returns:`, then `if r > 0:` indented once, then `count = count + 1` indented twice.

feedback.correct: All six tests passed, flat days and empty lists included.
feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Check a list of flat days, `[0.0, 0.0]`: it has 0 up days.

byKey.test-1: If test 1 got 4, you counted the 0.0 day. A return of exactly 0.0 is flat, not up: use `r > 0`, not `r >= 0`.

ideas: `for x in a_list:` runs its block once per item, with `x` holding each item in turn; an empty list gives zero passes.
`range(a, b)` gives a, a + 1, ..., b − 1: it stops before `b`, and `range(n)` starts at 0.
An accumulator starts once, before the loop, and is updated once per item inside it.

formula.name: Running total
formula.note: Start at 0, add each item; the sum of an empty list is 0.

summary.trap: Putting `total = 0` inside the loop resets it on every pass, leaving only the last item.

options.why: You started at 0. `range(2, 5)` starts at its first number, 2.
You printed how many numbers there are. The loop prints each one.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The first number is where it starts; the second is the first one left out.

explain.text: `range(2, 5)` gives 2, 3 and 4: it starts at 2 and stops before 5. That is 5 − 2 = 3 numbers.

quiz.question: How many lines does it print?

feedback.correct: Three passes print `check`; `report` prints once after the loop.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the passes, then look at the unindented line.

byKey.inside: You printed `report` on every pass. It is not indented, so it runs once, after the loop.
byKey.three: You missed `report`. It runs once, after the loop ends.

explain.text: The list has three items, so `check` prints three times. `report` is not indented, so it runs once after the loop: four lines.

quiz.prose:
```python
total = 0
for r in [1.5, -0.5, 2.0, -1.0]:
    if r < 0:
        total = total + r
print(total)
```
quiz.question: What does it print?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add only the values that pass `r < 0`.

byKey.all: You added every value. The `if` lets only negative returns into the total.
byKey.last: You kept only the last loss. `total` adds each negative return to what it already holds.
byKey.gains: You added the positive values. The test is `r < 0`, so only losses are added.

explain.text: Only −0.5 and −1.0 pass `r < 0`, so the total is −1.5. This sums the losing days: a first step towards measuring downside.

quiz.prose:
```python
total = 0
for p in []:
    total = total + p
print(total)
```
quiz.question: What happens?

options.text: It stops with an error, because the list is empty.
options.why: Looping over an empty list is allowed: the block simply runs zero times.
`print(total)` is outside the loop, so it runs once whatever the list holds.
`total` was set to 0 before the loop, and nothing changed it.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. How many passes does an empty list give?

explain.text: An empty list gives zero passes, so the block never runs and `total` keeps its starting value, 0. That is why the accumulator starts at 0: the sum of nothing is 0.
